\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Data.}
All synthetic data is generated by Qwen3-8B~\citep{qwen3_2025}.
The IID dataset contains 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, split into training (350), validation (74), and test (76) sets with balanced class ratios (e.g., test = 38 jailbreak + 38 benign).
Stage~1 (DAPT) uses training + validation conversations; Stage~2 (BiGRU) trains on training, early-stops on validation, and evaluates on test.
OOD evaluation pairs attack-specific jailbreak conversations with the 38 IID-test benign conversations: 80 FITD~\citep{fitd2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, and 80 ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} + 38 benign = 118 total.
No overlap exists in attack templates across families.
The OOD benign set is IID (same generation pipeline as training); the OOD challenge is in distinguishing novel attack families from familiar benign conversations.
A paraphrased version of the IID test set (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20) serves as the adversarial robustness benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
For human data validation, we use ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 jailbreak + 204 benign from real LMSYS user interactions), entirely independent of Qwen3-8B generation.

\paragraph{Models.}
Seven DeBERTa-v3 variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline and differ only in Stage-1 training (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Our vanilla DeBERTa+BiGRU configuration corresponds to the DeepContext architecture~\citep{deepcontext2026}, with DeBERTa-v3-base replacing BERT as the encoder and identical BiGRU temporal aggregation; it serves as our primary baseline.
For cross-encoder validation, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class variants on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
We also compare TF-IDF LR and LLM-as-judge baselines (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}): GPT-5.5 achieves only F1 = 0.191--0.449 on IID Crescendo with 30--47\% unparseable responses; on OOD data, zero-shot Qwen3-8B achieves macro F1 = 0.244 (DD and ActorAttack) by predicting nearly all conversations as benign, and even 3-shot prompting reaches only 0.566 (DD) and 0.652 (ActorAttack). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
F1 for binary jailbreak detection at prefix $K$=2 and full conversations (full per-$K$ results in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}).
OOD results report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456) for all variants.
For key pairwise comparisons, we report BCa bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples over individual predictions pooled across seeds) and paired permutation tests (10,000 permutations). Bootstrap means may differ slightly from seed-averaged F1 due to the nonlinearity of F1 aggregation.
All standard deviations are computed over 3 random seeds using the population formula ($n$ divisor); Bessel-corrected estimates ($n{-}1$ divisor) are $\approx$22\% larger but do not alter any significance conclusions.
Stage-1: learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch 16, 4 epochs, MLM masking 15\%.
Stage-2: two-layer MLP, 20 epochs.

Classification supervision provides a consistent stability benefit across both base encoders (cross-seed variance: 0.005--0.046 vs.\ 0.026--0.201).

CKA analysis~\citep{kornblith2019cka} and linear probing confirm that DAPT reshapes representations substantially, though comparable CKA shifts yield different detection gains across starting points (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_heatmap}).

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Human Data Validation}
\label{sec:human_data}

Since both training and OOD evaluation data are Qwen3-8B-generated, we validate on ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 human-written jailbreak attempts + 204 benign conversations from real LMSYS interactions).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering

All DAPT variants exceed vanilla by 18--42\,pp (Table~\ref{tab:human_data}), confirming that the adapted-vs.-vanilla gap is not a Qwen3-8B generation artifact: domain exposure on synthetic jailbreak text transfers to human-written attacks.

The relative ordering among domain-adapted variants differs from multi-turn evaluations: JB-MLM leads (0.837$\pm$0.013) while classification-supervised variants rank lower (9-class: 0.596$\pm$0.087). The reversal is statistically significant ($p < 0.001$, non-overlapping CIs).
ToxicChat contains single-turn attacks with no multi-turn escalation, so the classification head provides no advantage over unsupervised domain exposure. This is a modality mismatch: the multi-turn evidence hierarchy requires multi-turn human data to validate.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Perturbation Analysis}
\label{sec:perturbation}

Under adversarial paraphrasing (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20), classification-supervised variants achieve zero F1 degradation at full conversation length on IID and OOD DD, while non-adapted models degrade by $\sim$12\,pp (McNemar 9-class vs.\ vanilla $p < 0.001$ on OOD DD).
On ActorAttack, absolute robustness does not hold (9-class $\Delta$\,=\,$-$20.4$\pm$13.5\,pp), but perturbation narrows rather than closes the adapted vs.\ non-adapted gap (9-class perturbed F1 = 0.768 vs.\ vanilla 0.248, $p < 0.001$).
Absolute perturbation robustness is attack-family-dependent; DAPT's detection advantage persists under paraphrasing.
Full results in Appendix~\ref{sec:perturbation_full}.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Strategy Trajectory Analysis}
\label{sec:strategy}

The 9-class persuasion taxonomy provides interpretable characterization of known attack families ($\kappa$=0.78, $n$=50; Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Transition count matrices reveal distinct orchestration patterns: Crescendo cycles broadly across all strategy categories, FITD concentrates on Role$\to$Obfuscation, and DD on Emotion$\to$Obfuscation (Appendix~\ref{sec:strategy_full}).
On unseen attacks, strategy prediction degrades to near-random ($\kappa$=0.126 on OOD DD), consistent with the detection mechanism analysis: all classification-supervised variants achieve equivalent detection F1 (0.997--1.000) regardless of strategy prediction quality. Detection operates through domain-adapted \texttt{[CLS]} embeddings, not through strategy classification accuracy.

\begin{abstract}
Detecting unseen multi-turn jailbreaks requires no better labels and no new architecture: domain text exposure alone suffices.
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks spread adversarial intent across benign-seeming turns, and existing defenses fail to generalize across attack families.
We isolate the factors behind cross-attack generalization through controlled ablation: thirteen encoder configurations at three scales (125 to 355M parameters) decompose the contributions of domain exposure, classification supervision, label quality, and granularity on three out-of-distribution (OOD) attack families.
A single factor explains the gap: for base-size encoders, continued pretraining on domain text closes roughly 60 percentage points of the OOD gap without any labels. Label quality, granularity, and temporal modeling are non-factors.
A capacity-dependent pattern holds across scales: as model size grows, the set of attacks that require adaptation shrinks, until the largest encoder generalizes without adaptation.
Classification supervision reduces prediction variance on synthetic evaluations regardless of label correctness, but this benefit reverses on human-authored data: on ToxicChat, unsupervised domain exposure yields macro F1 0.84 versus 0.41 without adaptation.
These findings reframe multi-turn jailbreak detection as a domain adaptation problem rather than a supervised classification task.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Human Data Validation}
\label{sec:human_data}

Since both training and OOD evaluation data are Qwen3-8B-generated, we validate on ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 human-written jailbreak attempts + 204 benign conversations from real LMSYS interactions).

All DAPT variants exceed vanilla by 18--42\,pp (Table~\ref{tab:human_data}), confirming that the adapted-vs.-vanilla gap is not a Qwen3-8B generation artifact: domain exposure on synthetic jailbreak text transfers to human-written attacks.

The relative ordering among domain-adapted variants differs from multi-turn evaluations: JB-MLM leads (0.837$\pm$0.013) while classification-supervised variants rank lower (9-class: 0.596$\pm$0.087). The reversal is statistically significant ($p < 0.001$, non-overlapping CIs).
ToxicChat contains single-turn attacks with no multi-turn escalation, so the classification head provides no advantage over unsupervised domain exposure. This is a modality mismatch: the multi-turn evidence hierarchy requires multi-turn human data to validate.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Perturbation Analysis}
\label{sec:perturbation}

Under adversarial paraphrasing (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20), classification-supervised variants achieve zero F1 degradation at full conversation length on IID and OOD DD, while non-adapted models degrade by $\sim$12\,pp (McNemar 9-class vs.\ vanilla $p < 0.001$ on OOD DD).
On ActorAttack, absolute robustness does not hold (9-class $\Delta$\,=\,$-$20.4$\pm$13.5\,pp), but perturbation narrows rather than closes the adapted vs.\ non-adapted gap (9-class perturbed F1 = 0.768 vs.\ vanilla 0.248, $p < 0.001$).
Absolute perturbation robustness is attack-family-dependent; DAPT's detection advantage persists under paraphrasing.
Full results in Appendix~\ref{sec:perturbation_full}.

\subsection{Strategy Trajectory Analysis}
\label{sec:strategy}

The 9-class persuasion taxonomy provides interpretable characterization of known attack families ($\kappa$=0.78, $n$=50; Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Transition count matrices reveal distinct orchestration patterns: Crescendo cycles broadly across all strategy categories, FITD concentrates on Role$\to$Obfuscation, and DD on Emotion$\to$Obfuscation (Appendix~\ref{sec:strategy_full}).
On unseen attacks, strategy prediction degrades to near-random ($\kappa$=0.126 on OOD DD), consistent with the detection mechanism analysis: all classification-supervised variants achieve equivalent detection F1 (0.997--1.000) regardless of strategy prediction quality. Detection operates through domain-adapted \texttt{[CLS]} embeddings, not through strategy classification accuracy.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Data.}
All synthetic data is generated by Qwen3-8B~\citep{qwen3_2025}.
The IID dataset contains 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, split into training (350), validation (74), and test (76) sets with balanced class ratios (e.g., test = 38 jailbreak + 38 benign).
Stage~1 (DAPT) uses training + validation conversations; Stage~2 (BiGRU) trains on training, early-stops on validation, and evaluates on test.
OOD evaluation pairs attack-specific jailbreak conversations with the 38 IID-test benign conversations: 80 FITD~\citep{fitd2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, and 80 ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} + 38 benign = 118 total.
No overlap exists in attack templates across families.
The OOD benign set is IID (same generation pipeline as training); the OOD challenge is in distinguishing novel attack families from familiar benign conversations.
A paraphrased version of the IID test set (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20) serves as the adversarial robustness benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
For human data validation, we use ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 jailbreak + 204 benign from real LMSYS user interactions), entirely independent of Qwen3-8B generation.

\paragraph{Models.}
Seven DeBERTa-v3 variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline and differ only in Stage-1 training (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Our vanilla DeBERTa+BiGRU configuration corresponds to the DeepContext architecture~\citep{deepcontext2026}, with DeBERTa-v3-base replacing BERT as the encoder and identical BiGRU temporal aggregation; it serves as our primary baseline.
For cross-encoder validation, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class variants on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
We also compare TF-IDF LR and LLM-as-judge baselines (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}): GPT-5.5 achieves only F1 = 0.191--0.449 on IID Crescendo with 30--47\% unparseable responses; on OOD data, zero-shot Qwen3-8B achieves macro F1 = 0.244 (DD and ActorAttack) by predicting nearly all conversations as benign, and even 3-shot prompting reaches only 0.566 (DD) and 0.652 (ActorAttack). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
F1 for binary jailbreak detection at prefix $K$=2 and full conversations (full per-$K$ results in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}).
OOD results report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456) for all variants.
For key pairwise comparisons, we report BCa bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples over individual predictions pooled across seeds) and paired permutation tests (10,000 permutations). Bootstrap means may differ slightly from seed-averaged F1 due to the nonlinearity of F1 aggregation.
All standard deviations are computed over 3 random seeds using the population formula ($n$ divisor); Bessel-corrected estimates ($n{-}1$ divisor) are $\approx$22\% larger but do not alter any significance conclusions.
Stage-1: learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch 16, 4 epochs, MLM masking 15\%.
Stage-2: two-layer MLP, 20 epochs.

\paragraph{Temporal modeling.}
Three-seed evaluation on both DD and ActorAttack confirms that mean pooling matches BiGRU (F1 gap $\leq$ 1\,pp on full conversations, overlapping CIs); detection thus relies on per-turn representations rather than their sequential order.

\paragraph{Summary.}
For base-size encoders (125--184M), domain exposure is the primary mechanism for cross-attack detection; label correctness, label granularity, temporal modeling, and domain specificity are non-factors. Classification supervision provides a complementary stability benefit (variance reduced 4--20$\times$) but does not change the detection ceiling established by domain exposure. \subsection{Cross-Encoder Validation}
\label{sec:cross_encoder}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-encoder comparison on OOD Full (3-seed mean$\pm$std). DD = Deceptive Delight, AA = ActorAttack. Bold indicates best per encoder group.}

Vanilla & .981$\pm$.026 & .466$\pm$.163 \\
MLM & .987$\pm$.018 & .730$\pm$.201 \\
9-class & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} & \textbf{.939$\pm$.046} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{RoBERTa-large (355M)}} \\[2pt]
Vanilla & .927$\pm$.036 & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} \\
MLM & .884$\pm$.065 & .874$\pm$.014 \\
9-class & \textbf{.987$\pm$.004} & .946$\pm$.057 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

To test whether the evidence hierarchy depends on encoder choice, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Table~\ref{tab:cross_encoder}).
On DD, RoBERTa-base vanilla already achieves 0.981$\pm$0.026 (vs.\ DeBERTa 0.312$\pm$0.026), so DAPT adds only 1.3\,pp. ActorAttack exposes this as DD's simplicity: RoBERTa-base vanilla collapses to 0.466$\pm$0.163, a 51.5\,pp drop, while domain-adapted variants recover (9-class: 0.939$\pm$0.046).

RoBERTa-large (355M) reveals a capacity-DAPT interaction: while domain adaptation improves DD detection across all scales (+6\,pp for large, +69\,pp for DeBERTa), its effect on ActorAttack reverses for the largest encoder (vanilla 1.000 vs.\ 9-class 0.946). Smaller encoders (125--184M) require DAPT to bridge a 47--71\,pp gap. The MLM-only variant identifies the mechanism as representation drift: all forms of continued pretraining (MLM 0.874$\pm$0.014, 9-class 0.946$\pm$0.057) reduce ActorAttack performance relative to the frozen encoder (1.000$\pm$0.000); a learning rate control (Appendix~\ref{app:roberta_large_lr}) confirms this is not hyperparameter-dependent. On DD, classification DAPT still provides net benefit (+6\,pp) through structured signal that partially compensates for drift, while MLM DAPT lacks this structure (0.884$\pm$0.065 vs.\ 0.927$\pm$0.036).

Three encoder scales thus reveal a capacity-dependent pattern for the \emph{difficulty threshold}: DeBERTa-v3-base requires adaptation for all attacks, RoBERTa-base only for complex ones, and RoBERTa-large for none (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
Classification supervision provides a consistent stability benefit across both base encoders (cross-seed variance: 0.005--0.046 vs.\ 0.026--0.201).

CKA analysis~\citep{kornblith2019cka} and linear probing confirm that DAPT reshapes representations substantially, though comparable CKA shifts yield different detection gains across starting points (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_heatmap}).

Now I have a comprehensive view. Let me synthesize my review based on the Director's 5 requested focus areas:

### 1. Story Strength: "classification-based DAPT is the only universally robust adaptation method"

Wait — the paper has SHIFTED its story from this claim. Looking at the current paper text:
- The abstract says: "domain text exposure alone suffices" — NOT classification-based DAPT
- The introduction says: "domain-adaptive pretraining is the primary mechanism for base-size encoders" — domain exposure, not classification
- The conclusion says: "DAPT bridges ~60pp of the OOD gap without labels" — again domain exposure


There's a fundamental tension here: the paper_framing.md identifies the core claim as classification-based DAPT being uniquely robust across LLMs (the finding that MLM collapses on mixed data while the 9-class variant survives), but the actual paper narrative centers on domain exposure sufficiency as the primary message, with classification playing only a stabilizing role. These are two different stories competing for prominence.

Looking at what the introduction and conclusion actually emphasize—domain exposure closes ~60pp of the OOD gap without labels, classification merely stabilizes synthetic predictions without transferring to real data, and model capacity reduces adaptation needs—the paper is clearly positioning domain exposure as the main mechanism, not classification robustness. So the framing document and the paper's actual argument have drifted apart.

The cross-LLM experiments that would support the "classification-based DAPT is universally robust" claim are buried in the Discussion and appendix, not featured in the main narrative. And checking the paper text, there's no mention of the D055-D059 experiments at all.

Now I'm looking at which of those newer experiments actually made it into the paper. Most of them—calibration metrics, frozen probing variants, data efficiency comparisons, inference efficiency, length stratification, lambda ablation—don't appear anywhere. Only the mean pooling result and t-SNE visualization show up, and even those are mentioned in passing rather than as central evidence.

The lambda ablation is particularly interesting because the paper does mention testing different lambda values, but it tested them on the full end-to-end model, not on the Stage-1 alpha parameter like experiment 31 did. And while the strategy prediction section cites a kappa value, I need to verify whether that's actually from experiment 32 or 33 or if it's from something else entirely.

There's a real gap here—experiments like the cross-seed ensemble and frozen MLM probing could have strengthened the claims significantly if they'd been properly integrated into the narrative rather than left in the appendix.

Looking at what's missing, the calibration results from experiment 24 would be valuable for arguing practical deployment benefits, showing predictions are well-calibrated compared to the baseline. More critically, the frozen probing experiments reveal something mechanistically important: that Stage 1 DAPT creates strong representations on its own, and that MLM's performance gap comes from Stage 2 rather than Stage 1. The data efficiency result is also striking—maintaining strong performance with just 50 training samples demonstrates the approach's robustness.

On the practical side, inference speed of 82.5 conversations per second supports deployment feasibility. However, there's a significant limitation I need to flag: the turn count distributions don't overlap across classes, meaning a simple length-based classifier could trivially distinguish them. This needs to be disclosed. The lambda ablation is also revealing—setting the persuasion loss to zero actually improves E2E performance, which contradicts the auxiliary loss helping and instead supports the interpretation that domain exposure matters more than explicit classification. Finally, the ensemble results show that majority voting preserves correctness across seeds, with MLM benefiting most from this approach.

Now looking at the strategy prediction results with different checkpoints: switching from exp16 to plan_002 checkpoints dramatically reduces the out-of-distribution miss rate for AA from 63/41/66 down to 1/7/1. This is crucial for the strategy analysis. But I'm also identifying the major vulnerabilities a reviewer will exploit. The turn-count confound is the biggest one—non-overlapping conversation lengths between benign and jailbreak samples mean the model could be learning length patterns rather than content semantics, and the paper doesn't acknowledge this at all. Then there's the ToxicChat reversal issue undermining the domain exposure story.

On real human data, the method hierarchy flips completely, which contradicts the paper's main claim about domain exposure being the primary mechanism. The paper dismisses this as a modality mismatch, but that's exactly the problem—the approach loses its value proposition when applied to actual human data. And RoBERTa-large achieving perfect performance on ActorAttack without any adaptation raises a harder question: if a larger model solves this without the method, why is DisPeD necessary? The paper frames it as a capacity-dependent finding, but reviewers will just see it as "use a bigger model instead." I need to strengthen the cost-efficiency argument here, and exp29 data might help make that case.

The three most critical weaknesses are the turn-count confound that wasn't disclosed, the trivial separability of 500 synthetic Qwen-generated conversations with non-overlapping turn counts combined with the ToxicChat reversal suggesting the model captures spurious correlations rather than genuine jailbreak features, and the fact that RoBERTa-large's own results undermine the necessity of the method entirely.

The negative results section actually handles ablations well—scrambled labels still work, mean pooling matches BiGRU, binary classification performs like 9-class, and hyperparameter sensitivity is minimal—but I need to check whether the lambda insensitivity is really about Stage-1 alpha or something else.

There are 19 recent experimental findings that haven't made it into the paper: E2E lambda=0 being optimal suggests the persuasion auxiliary loss actually hurts, frozen MLM performs identically to frozen 9-class, frozen probing matches the full pipeline, mean pooling across all 24 metrics achieves perfect performance, and the data efficiency curve is completely flat. The MLM being Qwen-specific is buried in the Discussion rather than properly addressed, and the narrative consistency between the abstract's claim about domain text exposure and the actual classification results needs checking.

Looking at the paper's story arc, the abstract, introduction, experiments, and conclusion all align around three main findings, but there's a mismatch: the framing document claims classification-based DAPT is universally robust, yet the paper has evolved beyond this claim. The Director's first question specifically targets this assertion, but the paper no longer actually makes it. The writing style appears clean with proper dash usage throughout.

Now checking how well each contribution maps to its supporting sections—the decomposition work, capacity-dependent patterns, and distribution-specific effects all have corresponding experimental sections backing them up. However, the title promises to explain what makes multi-turn jailbreaks detectable through systematic decomposition, but the actual answer boils down to domain exposure on text, which isn't particularly novel. The method's real distinguishing contribution around the persuasion taxonomy seems to get lost in the framing.

Let me now pull together the full review against those five key areas the Director outlined, and I'm also cross-checking the reported numbers against what I saw in the experiments to make sure everything's consistent. I'm trying to track down where the 0.191 F1 score comes from — it might be a per-prefix result rather than the full score, since the appendix only shows 0.383 for the complete evaluation. The paper mentions this range multiple times, which suggests it could be referring to performance across different prefix lengths, though the exact breakdown isn't clear from what I'm seeing.

Now looking at the RoBERTa-large variants, I notice some striking differences in their performance metrics across the DD and AA tasks.

The vanilla RoBERTa-large achieves perfect AA performance (1.000±0.000), but both the MLM and 9-class DAPT variants actually degrade this score substantially — dropping to 0.874±0.014 and 0.946±0.057 respectively. Meanwhile, on DD, the 9-class variant improves from 0.927 to 0.987, so the adaptation helps there but hurts on ActorAttack. This creates a tension with the paper's introduction, which claims RoBERTa-large handles ActorAttack without adaptation (which is true at 1.000), yet still argues for DAPT as beneficial. There's also an inconsistency in how the paper frames the "capacity-dependent pattern" — it seems to conflate different model architectures rather than just different scales of the same architecture.

I'm also noticing several critical experiments from the D055-D059 range are completely absent from the paper: calibration analysis, frozen probing, data efficiency, inference efficiency, and length stratification. The length stratification experiment in particular seems like a major omission that could explain some of the confounding effects they're observing.

Now I need to cross-reference against the paper's provenance to see what's actually documented, then structure my review around the Director's five focus areas.

## 论文主正文通盘审查（§1-§6）

按 Director 要求的 5 个维度逐一评估，基于远程 .tex 文件独立阅读 + 所有 exp24-36 实验结果交叉验证。

---

### 1. Story 强度

**[severity: info]** 当前论文的叙事主线是 "domain exposure is the primary mechanism; classification adds stability on synthetic but not human data; capacity reduces the need for adaptation"。三贡献结构在 Abstract → Intro → Experiments → Discussion → Conclusion 之间逻辑链完整一致。

**[severity: warning]** paper_framing.md 的 Core Claim 仍然写着 "classification-based DAPT is the ONLY universally robust adaptation method"（D049 framing），但当前论文正文已经不讲这个故事。Introduction 将 classification 定位为 "complementary but narrower benefit"，Abstract 的 headline 是 "domain text exposure alone suffices"。两者矛盾。**建议**：同步更新 paper_framing.md 使其与论文实际 narrative 一致，避免后续 Paper Agent 引用过时 framing 写错章节。

---

### 2. Claim-Evidence 匹配（D055-D059 实验覆盖）

**[severity: warning]** D055-D059 新增的 ~12 个实验（exp24-36）中，仅 exp34（t-SNE）出现在 Appendix。以下实验的结果 **完全未被论文引用**：

| 实验 | 结果 | 论文状态 |
|------|------|----------|
| exp24 ECE 校准 | 9-class ECE 0.12-0.14 vs vanilla 0.50-0.67 | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp26 冻结 probing | AA OOD 0.972±0.026（≈ E2E 0.997） | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp28 数据效率 | N=50 AA 0.969±0.030 vs vanilla 0.234 | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp29 推理效率 | 12.12ms/conv, 82.5 conv/s | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp30 长度分层 | benign 12-20 turns, DD 6-10, AA 3-8（不重叠！） | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp31 E2E lambda | λ=0 最优，persuasion aux loss 有害 | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp33 策略预测 plan_002 | AA 漏检 1/7/1 vs exp32 的 63/41/66 | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp35 集成投票 | 从不破坏正确预测，MLM 获益最大 | ❌ 未引用 |
| exp36 冻结 MLM probing | AA 0.941±0.037（vs 冻结 9-class 0.972） | ❌ 未引用 |

这些实验中多个对论文 story 有直接支撑作用（见下方第 3 点），不写进去是实质性的 evidence gap。

---

### 3. 可加强的地方（通过引用新 ablation 结果）

**[severity: warning]** 以下是最高价值的加强机会：

**(a) exp26+exp36 冻结 probing → 机制证据核心**
冻结 9-class encoder + 随机 BiGRU 就能达到 AA OOD 0.972±0.026（≈ E2E 0.997），证明 Stage 1 DAPT 单独就创造了高质量表征。冻结 MLM encoder（0.941）> MLM full pipeline（0.893），揭示 MLM 的弱点来自 Stage 2 不稳定性而非 Stage 1 表征质量。这是支撑 "domain exposure is the mechanism" 叙事的**最强机制证据**，当前论文的 "CKA analysis and linear probing" 一句带过完全不够。建议在 Decomposition 段加一个 \paragraph{Representation quality} 段落，Appendix 放完整表格。

**(b) exp28 数据效率 → 实用性卖点**
仅 50 个训练样本就能达到 AA OOD 0.969±0.030（vs vanilla 0.234）。这是一个极强的 practical claim："50 conversations suffice for robust cross-attack detection"。可以在 Summary 段加一句，Appendix 放 N=50/125/250/350 曲线表。

**(c) exp31 E2E lambda → 直接支撑 decomposition 结论**
Stage-2 E2E fine-tuning中 λ=0（无 persuasion aux loss）在所有指标上最优，λ 增大单调降低 AA OOD 性能（0→2.0: AA 1.0→0.944）。这与 Stage-1 α insensitivity 是**不同层面的发现**——当前论文只说 "α∈{0,0.3,0.5,2.0} all F1=1.0"（Stage-1 on IID），未提 Stage-2 E2E lambda 结果。建议在 Decomposition 段补充。

**(d) exp29 推理效率 → 部署论证**
12.12ms/conv（DeBERTa+BiGRU）vs LLM-as-judge 2-5s estimated。一句话即可加入 Reproducibility Details 或 Conclusion 段。

---

### 4. 审稿人攻击面 Top 3

**[severity: critical] 攻击面 #1：Turn-count confound（exp30，未披露）**

exp30 发现 benign 对话 12-20 turns，DD jailbreak 6-10 turns，AA jailbreak 3-8 turns——三类之间 **turn count 完全不重叠**。这意味着一个简单的长度阈值分类器就能实现近乎完美的分类，无需任何内容分析。论文 **没有在任何地方披露** 这个 confound。

现有的部分缓解证据：(a) mean pooling ≈ BiGRU 说明模型不依赖序列顺序；(b) K=1/K=2 early detection 说明模型能从 1-2 turns 就检测，此时长度信息极弱；(c) 冻结 probing（exp26）也达到高 F1 说明 turn-level 表征质量而非序列长度驱动检测。但这些都是**间接证据**，论文必须**显式讨论**这个 confound 并引用上述缓解。一个细心的审稿人看到数据统计就会提出此问题——如果论文不主动讨论，会被视为隐瞒。

**建议**：在 Limitations 段新增一个 \paragraph{Turn-count distribution} 明确披露长度分布差异，列出缓解证据，并承认在长度匹配数据上的验证是未来工作。

**[severity: warning] 攻击面 #2：极小测试集 + 近天花板性能**

IID test = 76 samples，OOD = 118 samples。9-class/binary/scrambled/MLM 在 DD OOD 的差距是 0.003-0.083（即 0-10 个样本的差异）。论文报告了 BCa bootstrap CI 和 permutation test，统计方法正确，但**固有统计功效极低**。"All classification variants converge to equivalent performance (0.951-0.990, max gap 3.9pp)" 这个结论在 n=118 上 CI 极宽，审稿人可能质疑 decomposition 的 granularity 超出了数据的分辨率。

现有缓解：3-seed evaluation、bootstrap CI。但审稿人仍可能要求更大测试集或效应量分析。

**[severity: warning] 攻击面 #3：RoBERTa-large 结果削弱方法的必要性**

Table 4 显示 RoBERTa-large vanilla 在 ActorAttack 上达到 1.000±0.000——无需任何 adaptation。而且 DAPT 反而 **降低** 其 AA 性能（9-class 0.946，MLM 0.874）。论文将此框架为 "capacity-dependent pattern" 发现，但审稿人会直接问："Why not just use a bigger model?" 当前 Discussion 的 "Encoder capacity confound" 段正确承认了这不是 clean capacity comparison（不同架构/预训练目标），但 Introduction 的 Contribution 2 将其呈现为一个 clean pattern，存在 overclaim 风险。

**建议**：(a) Introduction 中将 "capacity-dependent pattern" 限定为 "suggestive" 而非确定性发现；(b) 引用 exp29 推理效率数据作为 cost argument（184M model + DAPT vs 355M model on computational budget）。

---

### 5. Negative 结果叙事整合

**[severity: warning]** 论文主正文整合了 4 个 negative 结果（scrambled=correct, binary≈9-class, mean_pooling≈BiGRU, alpha insensitive），叙事处理良好。但 D055-D059 新增的多个 negative 结果**完全未整合**：

- exp31 λ=0 最优 → persuasion aux loss 在 E2E 中有害（支撑 "domain exposure not classification" narrative）
- exp36 frozen MLM ≈ frozen 9-class（Δ=3.1pp < 5pp）→ DAPT 方法论对表征质量不重要（支撑同上）
- exp35 ensemble 从不破坏正确预测但 vanilla 太弱 → classification supervision 不能通过 post-hoc aggregation 弥补
- exp28 N=50 already sufficient → data efficiency flat curve 是一个 positive practical finding

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

\paragraph{Data.}
All synthetic data is generated by Qwen3-8B~\citep{qwen3_2025}.
The IID dataset contains 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, split into training (350), validation (74), and test (76) sets with balanced class ratios (e.g., test = 38 jailbreak + 38 benign).
Stage~1 (DAPT) uses training + validation conversations; Stage~2 (BiGRU) trains on training, early-stops on validation, and evaluates on test.
OOD evaluation pairs attack-specific jailbreak conversations with the 38 IID-test benign conversations: 80 FITD~\citep{fitd2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, and 80 ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} + 38 benign = 118 total.
No overlap exists in attack templates across families.
The OOD benign set is IID (same generation pipeline as training); the OOD challenge is in distinguishing novel attack families from familiar benign conversations.
A paraphrased version of the IID test set (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20) serves as the adversarial robustness benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
For human data validation, we use ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 jailbreak + 204 benign from real LMSYS user interactions), entirely independent of Qwen3-8B generation.

\paragraph{Models.}
Seven DeBERTa-v3 variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline and differ only in Stage-1 training (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Our vanilla DeBERTa+BiGRU configuration corresponds to the DeepContext architecture~\citep{deepcontext2026}, with DeBERTa-v3-base replacing BERT as the encoder and identical BiGRU temporal aggregation; it serves as our primary baseline.
For cross-encoder validation, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class variants on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
We also compare TF-IDF LR and LLM-as-judge baselines (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}): GPT-5.5 achieves only F1 = 0.191--0.449 on IID Crescendo with 30--47\% unparseable responses; on OOD data, zero-shot Qwen3-8B achieves macro F1 = 0.244 (DD and ActorAttack) by predicting nearly all conversations as benign, and even 3-shot prompting reaches only 0.566 (DD) and 0.652 (ActorAttack). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
F1 for binary jailbreak detection at prefix $K$=2 and full conversations (full per-$K$ results in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}).

1	% experiments.tex — D024 compressed for 8-page limit
2	
3	\section{Experiments}
4	
5	\subsection{Setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Data.}
8	All synthetic data is generated by Qwen3-8B~\citep{qwen3_2025}.
9	The IID dataset contains 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, split into training (350), validation (74), and test (76) sets with balanced class ratios (e.g., test = 38 jailbreak + 38 benign).
10	Stage~1 (DAPT) uses training + validation conversations; Stage~2 (BiGRU) trains on training, early-stops on validation, and evaluates on test.
11	OOD evaluation pairs attack-specific jailbreak conversations with the 38 IID-test benign conversations: 80 FITD~\citep{fitd2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, and 80 ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} + 38 benign = 118 total.
12	No overlap exists in attack templates across families.
13	The OOD benign set is IID (same generation pipeline as training); the OOD challenge is in distinguishing novel attack families from familiar benign conversations.
14	A paraphrased version of the IID test set (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20) serves as the adversarial robustness benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
15	For human data validation, we use ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 jailbreak + 204 benign from real LMSYS user interactions), entirely independent of Qwen3-8B generation.
16	
17	\paragraph{Models.}
18	Seven DeBERTa-v3 variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline and differ only in Stage-1 training (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
19	Our vanilla DeBERTa+BiGRU configuration is architecturally equivalent to DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026}, differing only in encoder choice (DeBERTa-v3-base vs.\ BERT); it serves as our primary baseline.
20	For cross-encoder validation, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class variants on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
21	We also compare TF-IDF LR and LLM-as-judge baselines (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}): GPT-5.5 achieves only F1 = 0.191--0.449 on IID Crescendo with 30--47\% unparseable responses; on OOD data, zero-shot Qwen3-8B achieves macro F1 = 0.244 (DD and ActorAttack) by predicting nearly all conversations as benign, and even 3-shot prompting reaches only 0.566 (DD) and 0.652 (ActorAttack). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.
22	
23	\paragraph{Metrics.}
24	F1 for binary jailbreak detection at prefix $K$=2 and full conversations (full per-$K$ results in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}).
25	OOD results report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456) for all variants.
26	For key pairwise comparisons, we report BCa bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples over individual predictions pooled across seeds) and paired permutation tests (10,000 permutations). Bootstrap means may differ slightly from seed-averaged F1 due to the nonlinearity of F1 aggregation.
27	All standard deviations are computed over 3 random seeds using the population formula ($n$ divisor); Bessel-corrected estimates ($n{-}1$ divisor) are $\approx$22\% larger but do not alter any significance conclusions.
28	Stage-1: learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch 16, 4 epochs, MLM masking 15\%.
29	Stage-2: two-layer MLP, 20 epochs.
30	
31	%----------------------------------------------------------------------
32	\subsection{Cross-Attack Generalization}
33	
34	\begin{table}[t]
35	\centering
36	\small
37	\caption{Cross-attack generalization (F1) at $K$=2 and full conversation length. IID: Crescendo; OOD: Deceptive Delight (DD). 3-seed mean$\pm$std where noted; full per-$K$ in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}.}
38	\label{tab:main_results}
39	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc|cc@{}}
40	\toprule
41	& \multicolumn{2}{c|}{\textit{IID (Cresc.)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textit{OOD (DD)}} \\
42	\textbf{Method} & $K$=2 & Full & $K$=2 & Full \\
43	\midrule
44	9-class & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & .981$\pm$.013 & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} \\
45	MLM-only$^{\ddagger}$ & .974 & 1.000 & \textbf{.993$\pm$.009} & .914$\pm$.115 \\
46	Vanilla & .978$\pm$.016 & 1.000$\pm$.000 & .479$\pm$.038 & .312$\pm$.026 \\
47	TF-IDF LR$^{\S}$ & 1.000 & 1.000 & 1.000 & .961 \\
48	\bottomrule
49	\end{tabular}
50	\vspace{-2pt}
51	{\footnotesize $^{\ddagger}$MLM-only IID reports single seed (42); OOD reports 3-seed. $^{\S}$TF-IDF is deterministic (no std).}
52	\end{table}
53	
54	Vanilla encoders collapse under cross-attack transfer; domain-adapted variants recover near-perfect detection (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:cross_attack_bar}).
55	DD exhibits high lexical separability (TF-IDF F1\,=\,0.961); ActorAttack, where TF-IDF collapses to 0.261, serves as the primary stress test for beyond-lexical generalization.
56	All methods achieve near-perfect IID F1, reflecting inherent lexical separability when test matches training.
57	On OOD DD, vanilla DeBERTa collapses to F1 = 0.312$\pm$0.026, worsening with more turns (0.628$\pm$0.038 at $K$=1 to 0.312$\pm$0.026 at Full), consistent with the finding that attack turns occupy ``benign'' embedding regions~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}.
58	MLM achieves mean F1 $\geq$ 0.97 at all prefixes $K \leq 5$ without any classification labels; domain exposure alone is sufficient.
59	At full conversation length, MLM drops to 0.914$\pm$0.115 (seed 456 recall = 0.64), while the 9-class model maintains 0.994$\pm$0.005.
60	TF-IDF LR reaches F1 = 0.961 on full DD with near-perfect per-prefix performance ($K$=1--5: 0.994--1.000); DD is thus fully solvable by lexical features alone.
61	On structurally complex ActorAttack, TF-IDF collapses to F1 = 0.261 (precision = 1.0, recall = 0.15), while 9-class maintains 0.972$\pm$0.026: a 71\,pp gap. Lexical methods cannot capture multi-persona role-playing attack structure. This establishes a ``difficulty threshold'' for lexical methods parallel to that of vanilla encoders: both succeed on DD and fail on ActorAttack (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
62	Bootstrap CIs confirm non-overlapping intervals (9-class DD Full [0.943, 1.000] vs.\ vanilla [0.202, 0.341]; all permutation $p < 0.0001$). FITD is non-discriminative (all variants F1\,$\geq$\,0.990; Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
63	
64	\begin{figure}[t]
65	\centering
66	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/paper/fig2_cross_attack_bar.pdf}
67	\caption{Cross-attack overview (F1 at full conversation length). DisPeD (9-class) maintains near-perfect detection across IID and both OOD families. Vanilla DeBERTa collapses on OOD Deceptive Delight, confirming the necessity of domain-adaptive pretraining. FITD is non-discriminative for all methods (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).}
68	\label{fig:cross_attack_bar}
69	\end{figure}
70	
71	Prefix-length analysis (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:full_prefix}) shows vanilla F1 drops from 0.628 at $K$=1 to 0.312 at full length. MLM achieves strong early detection ($K$=2: 0.993) but is unstable at full length (0.914$\pm$0.115); the 9-class model maintains 0.972--0.994 across all prefixes, demonstrating that classification supervision stabilizes against distributional drift.
72	
73	%----------------------------------------------------------------------
74	\subsection{Decomposing the Detection Mechanism}
75	\label{sec:decomposition}
76	
77	\begin{table}[t]
78	\centering
79	\small
80	\caption{Evidence hierarchy on OOD DD and ActorAttack (AA) at full conversation length (3-seed mean$\pm$std where available). Bold indicates best per column. All variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline. Full per-prefix results in Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:full_prefix} and~\ref{tab:actorattack_full}.}
81	\label{tab:evidence_hierarchy}
82	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
83	\toprule
84	\textbf{Variant} & DD-Full & AA-Full & DD-$K$=2 \\
85	\midrule
86	9-class (full model) & .994$\pm$.005 & .972$\pm$.026 & .981$\pm$.013 \\
87	Binary (2-class) & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{.990$\pm$.008} & .994$\pm$.009 \\
88	Scrambled labels & .994$\pm$.005 & .951$\pm$.043 & .981$\pm$.026 \\
89	MLM-only$^{\ddagger}$ (no labels) & .914$\pm$.115 & .893$\pm$.080 & .993$\pm$.009 \\
90	Mean pooling$^{*}$ & .991$\pm$.013 & .962$\pm$.015 & \textbf{1.000} \\
91	\midrule
92	Topic classif.\ (5-class) & .541$\pm$.207 & .625$\pm$.141 & .593$\pm$.166 \\
93	Wikipedia MLM & .904$\pm$.115 & .686$\pm$.297 & .911$\pm$.073 \\
94	Vanilla DeBERTa & .312$\pm$.026 & .258$\pm$.000 & .479$\pm$.038 \\
95	TF-IDF LR$^{\dagger}$ & .961 & .261 & \textbf{1.000} \\
96	\bottomrule
97	\end{tabular}
98	\vspace{-2pt}
99	{\footnotesize $^{*}$9-class encoder with mean pooling replacing BiGRU. $^{\dagger}$Deterministic (no std). $^{\ddagger}$MLM-only IID (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}) is single-seed (42); all OOD values are 3-seed.}
100	\end{table}
101	
102	A clear \emph{evidence hierarchy} emerges across seven variants (Table~\ref{tab:evidence_hierarchy}), ordered by OOD detection at full conversation length on DD:
103	
104	\vspace{2pt}
105	\noindent\hspace{0.5em}{\small vanilla (0.312$\pm$0.026) $<$ topic (0.541$\pm$0.207) $\ll$ wiki-MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115) $\approx$ jb-MLM (0.914$\pm$0.115) $<$ scrambled (0.994$\pm$0.005) $=$ 9-class (0.994$\pm$0.005) $\approx$ binary (1.000$\pm$0.000)}
106	\vspace{2pt}
107	
108	\paragraph{Domain exposure is the primary mechanism.}
109	MLM bridges $\sim$60\,pp from vanilla (0.312$\pm$0.026 $\to$ 0.914$\pm$0.115) without labels; this supports the DAPT interpretation~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}. TF-IDF collapse on ActorAttack (0.261 vs.\ 9-class 0.972) confirms that domain-adapted representations capture features beyond lexical overlap.
110	All three classification-supervised variants converge to equivalent detection (F1 = 0.994--1.000); McNemar's test finds no significant pairwise differences (all $p > 0.13$; $\leq$7 discordant pairs limit power), and paired permutation tests confirm equivalence ($p \geq 0.40$). TOST equivalence tests (margin = 5\,pp) confirm statistical equivalence on DD (all $p < 0.01$, 90\% CI within $\pm$0.05), robust to $\delta$=2\,pp ($p$=0.035; Table~\ref{tab:tost_sensitivity}). On ActorAttack, the mean gap is 2.1\,pp (within noise at $n$=3) but TOST is underpowered (SE\,=\,0.045) to confirm formal equivalence; descriptively similar but formally inconclusive. Label quality and granularity are non-factors for detection.
111	Classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance 4--20$\times$ over MLM on synthetic OOD (std 0.005 vs.\ 0.115 on DD; observed across 3 seeds, suggestive but not conclusive). This stability benefit does not transfer to human-authored data, where classification-supervised variants exhibit the highest variance and pure MLM the lowest (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}).
112	Appendix~\ref{app:tsne} provides t-SNE visualizations confirming that domain-adapted variants produce tighter, more separable embedding clusters than the vanilla baseline.
113	
114	\paragraph{Domain specificity is marginal at full length but meaningful for early detection.}
115	Wikipedia MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115) nearly matches jailbreak-domain MLM at full length (1\,pp gap), though jailbreak-domain text provides an 8\,pp advantage at early prefixes ($K$=2: 0.993 vs.\ 0.911).
116	Perturbation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}) reveals a sharper domain specificity effect: Wikipedia MLM degrades by $\sim$12\,pp under adversarial paraphrasing while jailbreak-domain MLM degrades by only 2.6\,pp.
117	
118	\paragraph{Misaligned supervision destabilizes generalization.}
119	Topic classification yields DD-Full F1 = 0.541$\pm$0.207; seed 123 falls \emph{below} vanilla (0.252 vs.\ 0.312). Despite using the same jailbreak-domain training data, topic classification performs worse than Wikipedia MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115), which uses out-of-domain text with no labels. A misaligned objective forces the encoder to allocate capacity to irrelevant features and actively destabilizes representations that MLM would preserve.
120	
121	\paragraph{Evidence hierarchy on structurally complex attacks.}
122	ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} uses multi-persona steering across longer conversation structures and provides a more challenging OOD benchmark than DD.
123	The evidence hierarchy at full conversation length is:
124	
125	\vspace{2pt}
126	\noindent\hspace{0.5em}{\small TF-IDF (0.261) $\approx$ vanilla (0.258$\pm$0.000) $<$ topic (0.625$\pm$0.141) $<$ wiki-MLM (0.686$\pm$0.297) $<$ jb-MLM (0.893$\pm$0.080) $<$ scrambled (0.951$\pm$0.043) $\approx$ 9-class (0.972$\pm$0.026) $\approx$ binary (0.990$\pm$0.008)}
127	\vspace{2pt}
128	
129	TF-IDF collapses from 0.961 (DD) to 0.261 (ActorAttack, precision = 1.0, recall = 0.15). This gap shows that domain-adapted representations capture features beyond bag-of-words.
130	All classification-supervised variants converge to equivalent performance (0.951--0.990, max gap 3.9\,pp); this extends the DD finding. DAPT provides $\sim$71\,pp over both vanilla (0.258) and TF-IDF (0.261). Full per-prefix results in Appendix~\ref{sec:actorattack_full}.
131	
132	\paragraph{Temporal modeling.}
133	Mean pooling matches BiGRU on both DD and ActorAttack (F1 gap $\leq$ 1\,pp, overlapping CIs; Appendix~\ref{app:temporal}).
134	Turn-order shuffling produces negligible change ($|\Delta| < 1$\,pp) across both DeBERTa-v3-base 9-class (DD $\Delta$\,=\,0.000, AA $\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.009, IID $\Delta$\,=\,0.000) and RoBERTa-large 9-class (DD $\Delta$\,=\,+0.001, AA $\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.007, IID $\Delta$\,=\,0.000), confirming that detection relies on per-turn representations rather than sequential patterns.
135	
136	\paragraph{Summary.}
137	For base-size encoders (125--184M), domain exposure is the primary mechanism; label correctness, granularity, temporal modeling, and domain specificity are non-factors. Classification supervision provides a complementary stability benefit (variance reduced 4--20$\times$) without changing the detection ceiling.
138	DD and FITD confirm that domain-adapted representations do not regress on easier attacks; ActorAttack provides the discriminative evaluation where lexical methods and vanilla encoders fail.
139	Detection is stable across conversation lengths (Appendix~\ref{app:length}) and near-saturates at 50 training conversations (Appendix~\ref{app:data_efficiency}).
140	
141	%----------------------------------------------------------------------
142	\subsection{Cross-Encoder Validation}
143	\label{sec:cross_encoder}
144	
145	\begin{table}[t]
146	\centering
147	\small
148	\caption{Cross-encoder comparison on OOD Full (3-seed mean$\pm$std). DD = Deceptive Delight, AA = ActorAttack. Bold indicates best per encoder group.}
149	\label{tab:cross_encoder}
150	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
151	\toprule
152	\textbf{Variant} & DD & AA \\
153	\midrule
154	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{DeBERTa-v3-base (184M)}} \\[2pt]
155	Vanilla & .312$\pm$.026 & .258$\pm$.000 \\
156	MLM & .914$\pm$.115 & .893$\pm$.080 \\
157	9-class & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} & \textbf{.972$\pm$.026} \\
158	\midrule
159	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{RoBERTa-base (125M)}} \\[2pt]
160	Vanilla & .981$\pm$.026 & .466$\pm$.163 \\
161	MLM & .987$\pm$.018 & .730$\pm$.201 \\
162	9-class & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} & \textbf{.939$\pm$.046} \\
163	\midrule
164	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{RoBERTa-large (355M)}} \\[2pt]
165	Vanilla & .927$\pm$.036 & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} \\
166	MLM & .884$\pm$.065 & .874$\pm$.014 \\
167	9-class & \textbf{.987$\pm$.004} & .946$\pm$.057 \\
168	\bottomrule
169	\end{tabular}
170	\end{table}
171	
172	To test whether the evidence hierarchy depends on encoder choice, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Table~\ref{tab:cross_encoder}).
173	On DD, RoBERTa-base vanilla already achieves 0.981$\pm$0.026 (vs.\ DeBERTa 0.312$\pm$0.026), so DAPT adds only 1.3\,pp. ActorAttack exposes this as DD's simplicity: RoBERTa-base vanilla collapses to 0.466$\pm$0.163, a 51.5\,pp drop, while domain-adapted variants recover (9-class: 0.939$\pm$0.046).
174	
175	RoBERTa-large (355M) reveals a capacity-DAPT interaction: its effect on ActorAttack reverses (vanilla 1.000 vs.\ 9-class 0.946), while smaller encoders require DAPT to bridge 47--71\,pp. All continued pretraining reduces ActorAttack performance for the largest encoder via representation drift (Table~\ref{tab:roberta_large_lr}), though classification DAPT partially compensates on DD (+6\,pp).
176	
177	Three encoder scales thus reveal a capacity-dependent observation for the \emph{difficulty threshold}: DeBERTa-v3-base requires adaptation for all attacks, RoBERTa-base only for complex ones, and RoBERTa-large for none (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
178	Classification supervision provides a consistent stability benefit across both base encoders (cross-seed variance: 0.005--0.046 vs.\ 0.026--0.201).
179	A BERT-base-uncased proxy (110M, matching DeepContext's encoder family) without adaptation achieves DD\,=\,0.318$\pm$0.031 and AA\,=\,0.275$\pm$0.027, comparable to vanilla DeBERTa-v3 (Appendix~\ref{app:bert_proxy}), confirming that cross-attack generalization is driven by DAPT rather than encoder architecture.
180	
181	CKA analysis~\citep{kornblith2019cka} and linear probing confirm that DAPT reshapes representations substantially (Figure~\ref{fig:cka_heatmap}), though comparable CKA shifts yield different detection gains across starting points (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_heatmap}).
182	
183	%----------------------------------------------------------------------

% experiments.tex — D024 compressed for 8-page limit

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

\paragraph{Data.}
All synthetic data is generated by Qwen3-8B~\citep{qwen3_2025}.
The IID dataset contains 250 Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo} jailbreak and 250 topic-anchored benign conversations, split into training (350), validation (74), and test (76) sets with balanced class ratios (e.g., test = 38 jailbreak + 38 benign).
Stage~1 (DAPT) uses training + validation conversations; Stage~2 (BiGRU) trains on training, early-stops on validation, and evaluates on test.
OOD evaluation pairs attack-specific jailbreak conversations with the 38 IID-test benign conversations: 80 FITD~\citep{fitd2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, 80 Deceptive Delight (DD)~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} + 38 benign = 118 total, and 80 ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} + 38 benign = 118 total.
No overlap exists in attack templates across families.
The OOD benign set is IID (same generation pipeline as training); the OOD challenge is in distinguishing novel attack families from familiar benign conversations.
A paraphrased version of the IID test set (BERTScore 0.92, lexical overlap 0.20) serves as the adversarial robustness benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}).
For human data validation, we use ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 jailbreak + 204 benign from real LMSYS user interactions), entirely independent of Qwen3-8B generation.

\paragraph{Models.}
Seven DeBERTa-v3 variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline and differ only in Stage-1 training (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
Our vanilla DeBERTa+BiGRU configuration is architecturally equivalent to DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026}, differing only in encoder choice (DeBERTa-v3-base vs.\ BERT); it serves as our primary baseline.
For cross-encoder validation, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class variants on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
We also compare TF-IDF LR and LLM-as-judge baselines (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}): GPT-5.5 achieves only F1 = 0.191--0.449 on IID Crescendo with 30--47\% unparseable responses; on OOD data, zero-shot Qwen3-8B achieves macro F1 = 0.244 (DD and ActorAttack) by predicting nearly all conversations as benign, and even 3-shot prompting reaches only 0.566 (DD) and 0.652 (ActorAttack). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
F1 for binary jailbreak detection at prefix $K$=2 and full conversations (full per-$K$ results in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}).
OOD results report 3-seed mean$\pm$std (seeds 42, 123, 456) for all variants.
For key pairwise comparisons, we report BCa bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples over individual predictions pooled across seeds) and paired permutation tests (10,000 permutations). Bootstrap means may differ slightly from seed-averaged F1 due to the nonlinearity of F1 aggregation.
All standard deviations are computed over 3 random seeds using the population formula ($n$ divisor); Bessel-corrected estimates ($n{-}1$ divisor) are $\approx$22\% larger but do not alter any significance conclusions.
Stage-1: learning rate $2 \times 10^{-5}$, batch 16, 4 epochs, MLM masking 15\%.
Stage-2: two-layer MLP, 20 epochs.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-Attack Generalization}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-attack generalization (F1) at $K$=2 and full conversation length. IID: Crescendo; OOD: Deceptive Delight (DD). 3-seed mean$\pm$std where noted; full per-$K$ in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_prefix}.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc|cc@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{2}{c|}{\textit{IID (Cresc.)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textit{OOD (DD)}} \\
\textbf{Method} & $K$=2 & Full & $K$=2 & Full \\
\midrule
9-class & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & .981$\pm$.013 & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} \\
MLM-only$^{\ddagger}$ & .974 & 1.000 & \textbf{.993$\pm$.009} & .914$\pm$.115 \\
Vanilla & .978$\pm$.016 & 1.000$\pm$.000 & .479$\pm$.038 & .312$\pm$.026 \\
TF-IDF LR$^{\S}$ & 1.000 & 1.000 & 1.000 & .961 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{-2pt}
{\footnotesize $^{\ddagger}$MLM-only IID reports single seed (42); OOD reports 3-seed. $^{\S}$TF-IDF is deterministic (no std).}
\end{table}

Vanilla encoders collapse under cross-attack transfer; domain-adapted variants recover near-perfect detection (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, Figure~\ref{fig:cross_attack_bar}).
DD exhibits high lexical separability (TF-IDF F1\,=\,0.961); ActorAttack, where TF-IDF collapses to 0.261, serves as the primary stress test for beyond-lexical generalization.
All methods achieve near-perfect IID F1, reflecting inherent lexical separability when test matches training.
On OOD DD, vanilla DeBERTa collapses to F1 = 0.312$\pm$0.026, worsening with more turns (0.628$\pm$0.038 at $K$=1 to 0.312$\pm$0.026 at Full), consistent with the finding that attack turns occupy ``benign'' embedding regions~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}.
MLM achieves mean F1 $\geq$ 0.97 at all prefixes $K \leq 5$ without any classification labels; domain exposure alone is sufficient.
At full conversation length, MLM drops to 0.914$\pm$0.115 (seed 456 recall = 0.64), while the 9-class model maintains 0.994$\pm$0.005.
TF-IDF LR reaches F1 = 0.961 on full DD with near-perfect per-prefix performance ($K$=1--5: 0.994--1.000); DD is thus fully solvable by lexical features alone.
On structurally complex ActorAttack, TF-IDF collapses to F1 = 0.261 (precision = 1.0, recall = 0.15), while 9-class maintains 0.972$\pm$0.026: a 71\,pp gap. Lexical methods cannot capture multi-persona role-playing attack structure. This establishes a ``difficulty threshold'' for lexical methods parallel to that of vanilla encoders: both succeed on DD and fail on ActorAttack (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
Bootstrap CIs confirm non-overlapping intervals (9-class DD Full [0.943, 1.000] vs.\ vanilla [0.202, 0.341]; all permutation $p < 0.0001$). FITD is non-discriminative (all variants F1\,$\geq$\,0.990; Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/paper/fig2_cross_attack_bar.pdf}
\caption{Cross-attack overview (F1 at full conversation length). DisPeD (9-class) maintains near-perfect detection across IID and both OOD families. Vanilla DeBERTa collapses on OOD Deceptive Delight, confirming the necessity of domain-adaptive pretraining. FITD is non-discriminative for all methods (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).}
\label{fig:cross_attack_bar}
\end{figure}

Prefix-length analysis (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:full_prefix}) shows vanilla F1 drops from 0.628 at $K$=1 to 0.312 at full length. MLM achieves strong early detection ($K$=2: 0.993) but is unstable at full length (0.914$\pm$0.115); the 9-class model maintains 0.972--0.994 across all prefixes, demonstrating that classification supervision stabilizes against distributional drift.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Decomposing the Detection Mechanism}
\label{sec:decomposition}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Evidence hierarchy on OOD DD and ActorAttack (AA) at full conversation length (3-seed mean$\pm$std where available). Bold indicates best per column. All variants share the same Stage-2 pipeline. Full per-prefix results in Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:full_prefix} and~\ref{tab:actorattack_full}.}
\label{tab:evidence_hierarchy}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & DD-Full & AA-Full & DD-$K$=2 \\
\midrule
9-class (full model) & .994$\pm$.005 & .972$\pm$.026 & .981$\pm$.013 \\
Binary (2-class) & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} & \textbf{.990$\pm$.008} & .994$\pm$.009 \\
Scrambled labels & .994$\pm$.005 & .951$\pm$.043 & .981$\pm$.026 \\
MLM-only$^{\ddagger}$ (no labels) & .914$\pm$.115 & .893$\pm$.080 & .993$\pm$.009 \\
Mean pooling$^{*}$ & .991$\pm$.013 & .962$\pm$.015 & \textbf{1.000} \\
\midrule
Topic classif.\ (5-class) & .541$\pm$.207 & .625$\pm$.141 & .593$\pm$.166 \\
Wikipedia MLM & .904$\pm$.115 & .686$\pm$.297 & .911$\pm$.073 \\
Vanilla DeBERTa & .312$\pm$.026 & .258$\pm$.000 & .479$\pm$.038 \\
TF-IDF LR$^{\dagger}$ & .961 & .261 & \textbf{1.000} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{-2pt}
{\footnotesize $^{*}$9-class encoder with mean pooling replacing BiGRU. $^{\dagger}$Deterministic (no std). $^{\ddagger}$MLM-only IID (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}) is single-seed (42); all OOD values are 3-seed.}
\end{table}

A clear \emph{evidence hierarchy} emerges across seven variants (Table~\ref{tab:evidence_hierarchy}), ordered by OOD detection at full conversation length on DD:

\vspace{2pt}
\noindent\hspace{0.5em}{\small vanilla (0.312$\pm$0.026) $<$ topic (0.541$\pm$0.207) $\ll$ wiki-MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115) $\approx$ jb-MLM (0.914$\pm$0.115) $<$ scrambled (0.994$\pm$0.005) $=$ 9-class (0.994$\pm$0.005) $\approx$ binary (1.000$\pm$0.000)}
\vspace{2pt}

\paragraph{Domain exposure is the primary mechanism.}
MLM bridges $\sim$60\,pp from vanilla (0.312$\pm$0.026 $\to$ 0.914$\pm$0.115) without labels; this supports the DAPT interpretation~\citep{gururangan2020dontstop}. TF-IDF collapse on ActorAttack (0.261 vs.\ 9-class 0.972) confirms that domain-adapted representations capture features beyond lexical overlap.
All three classification-supervised variants converge to equivalent detection (F1 = 0.994--1.000); McNemar's test finds no significant pairwise differences (all $p > 0.13$; $\leq$7 discordant pairs limit power), and paired permutation tests confirm equivalence ($p \geq 0.40$). TOST equivalence tests (margin = 5\,pp) confirm statistical equivalence on DD (all $p < 0.01$, 90\% CI within $\pm$0.05), robust to $\delta$=2\,pp ($p$=0.035; Table~\ref{tab:tost_sensitivity}). On ActorAttack, the mean gap is 2.1\,pp (within noise at $n$=3) but TOST is underpowered (SE\,=\,0.045) to confirm formal equivalence; descriptively similar but formally inconclusive. Label quality and granularity are non-factors for detection.
Classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance 4--20$\times$ over MLM on synthetic OOD (std 0.005 vs.\ 0.115 on DD; observed across 3 seeds, suggestive but not conclusive). This stability benefit does not transfer to human-authored data, where classification-supervised variants exhibit the highest variance and pure MLM the lowest (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}).
Appendix~\ref{app:tsne} provides t-SNE visualizations confirming that domain-adapted variants produce tighter, more separable embedding clusters than the vanilla baseline.

\paragraph{Domain specificity is marginal at full length but meaningful for early detection.}
Wikipedia MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115) nearly matches jailbreak-domain MLM at full length (1\,pp gap), though jailbreak-domain text provides an 8\,pp advantage at early prefixes ($K$=2: 0.993 vs.\ 0.911).
Perturbation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:perturbation}) reveals a sharper domain specificity effect: Wikipedia MLM degrades by $\sim$12\,pp under adversarial paraphrasing while jailbreak-domain MLM degrades by only 2.6\,pp.

\paragraph{Misaligned supervision destabilizes generalization.}
Topic classification yields DD-Full F1 = 0.541$\pm$0.207; seed 123 falls \emph{below} vanilla (0.252 vs.\ 0.312). Despite using the same jailbreak-domain training data, topic classification performs worse than Wikipedia MLM (0.904$\pm$0.115), which uses out-of-domain text with no labels. A misaligned objective forces the encoder to allocate capacity to irrelevant features and actively destabilizes representations that MLM would preserve.

\paragraph{Evidence hierarchy on structurally complex attacks.}
ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} uses multi-persona steering across longer conversation structures and provides a more challenging OOD benchmark than DD.
The evidence hierarchy at full conversation length is:

\vspace{2pt}
\noindent\hspace{0.5em}{\small TF-IDF (0.261) $\approx$ vanilla (0.258$\pm$0.000) $<$ topic (0.625$\pm$0.141) $<$ wiki-MLM (0.686$\pm$0.297) $<$ jb-MLM (0.893$\pm$0.080) $<$ scrambled (0.951$\pm$0.043) $\approx$ 9-class (0.972$\pm$0.026) $\approx$ binary (0.990$\pm$0.008)}
\vspace{2pt}

TF-IDF collapses from 0.961 (DD) to 0.261 (ActorAttack, precision = 1.0, recall = 0.15). This gap shows that domain-adapted representations capture features beyond bag-of-words.
All classification-supervised variants converge to equivalent performance (0.951--0.990, max gap 3.9\,pp); this extends the DD finding. DAPT provides $\sim$71\,pp over both vanilla (0.258) and TF-IDF (0.261). Full per-prefix results in Appendix~\ref{sec:actorattack_full}.

\paragraph{Temporal modeling.}
Mean pooling matches BiGRU on both DD and ActorAttack (F1 gap $\leq$ 1\,pp, overlapping CIs; Appendix~\ref{app:temporal}).
Turn-order shuffling produces negligible change ($|\Delta| < 1$\,pp) across both DeBERTa-v3-base 9-class (DD $\Delta$\,=\,0.000, AA $\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.009, IID $\Delta$\,=\,0.000) and RoBERTa-large 9-class (DD $\Delta$\,=\,+0.001, AA $\Delta$\,=\,$-$0.007, IID $\Delta$\,=\,0.000), confirming that detection relies on per-turn representations rather than sequential patterns.

\paragraph{Summary.}
For base-size encoders (125--184M), domain exposure is the primary mechanism; label correctness, granularity, temporal modeling, and domain specificity are non-factors. Classification supervision provides a complementary stability benefit (variance reduced 4--20$\times$) without changing the detection ceiling.
DD and FITD confirm that domain-adapted representations do not regress on easier attacks; ActorAttack provides the discriminative evaluation where lexical methods and vanilla encoders fail.
Detection is stable across conversation lengths (Appendix~\ref{app:length}) and near-saturates at 50 training conversations (Appendix~\ref{app:data_efficiency}).

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-Encoder Validation}
\label{sec:cross_encoder}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-encoder comparison on OOD Full (3-seed mean$\pm$std). DD = Deceptive Delight, AA = ActorAttack. Bold indicates best per encoder group.}
\label{tab:cross_encoder}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & DD & AA \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{DeBERTa-v3-base (184M)}} \\[2pt]
Vanilla & .312$\pm$.026 & .258$\pm$.000 \\
MLM & .914$\pm$.115 & .893$\pm$.080 \\
9-class & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} & \textbf{.972$\pm$.026} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{RoBERTa-base (125M)}} \\[2pt]
Vanilla & .981$\pm$.026 & .466$\pm$.163 \\
MLM & .987$\pm$.018 & .730$\pm$.201 \\
9-class & \textbf{.994$\pm$.005} & \textbf{.939$\pm$.046} \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{RoBERTa-large (355M)}} \\[2pt]
Vanilla & .927$\pm$.036 & \textbf{1.000$\pm$.000} \\
MLM & .884$\pm$.065 & .874$\pm$.014 \\
9-class & \textbf{.987$\pm$.004} & .946$\pm$.057 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

To test whether the evidence hierarchy depends on encoder choice, we replicate vanilla, MLM, and 9-class on RoBERTa-base~\citep{liu2019roberta} (Table~\ref{tab:cross_encoder}).
On DD, RoBERTa-base vanilla already achieves 0.981$\pm$0.026 (vs.\ DeBERTa 0.312$\pm$0.026), so DAPT adds only 1.3\,pp. ActorAttack exposes this as DD's simplicity: RoBERTa-base vanilla collapses to 0.466$\pm$0.163, a 51.5\,pp drop, while domain-adapted variants recover (9-class: 0.939$\pm$0.046).

RoBERTa-large (355M) reveals a capacity-DAPT interaction: its effect on ActorAttack reverses (vanilla 1.000 vs.\ 9-class 0.946), while smaller encoders require DAPT to bridge 47--71\,pp. All continued pretraining reduces ActorAttack performance for the largest encoder via representation drift (Table~\ref{tab:roberta_large_lr}), though classification DAPT partially compensates on DD (+6\,pp).

Three encoder scales thus reveal a capacity-dependent observation for the \emph{difficulty threshold}: DeBERTa-v3-base requires adaptation for all attacks, RoBERTa-base only for complex ones, and RoBERTa-large for none (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
Classification supervision provides a consistent stability benefit across both base encoders (cross-seed variance: 0.005--0.046 vs.\ 0.026--0.201).
A BERT-base-uncased proxy (110M, matching DeepContext's encoder family) without adaptation achieves DD\,=\,0.318$\pm$0.031 and AA\,=\,0.275$\pm$0.027, comparable to vanilla DeBERTa-v3 (Appendix~\ref{app:bert_proxy}), confirming that cross-attack generalization is driven by DAPT rather than encoder architecture.

CKA analysis~\citep{kornblith2019cka} and linear probing confirm that DAPT reshapes representations substantially (Figure~\ref{fig:cka_heatmap}), though comparable CKA shifts yield different detection gains across starting points (Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_heatmap}).

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Mixed-LLM Training}

All preceding experiments use single-source (Qwen3-8B) data. To test whether the evidence hierarchy transfers when training data mixes LLM sources, we train on 250 Qwen + 250 Llama-3.1-8B conversations (Table~\ref{tab:mixed_llm}).
Classification-based DAPT is the only variant that substantially outperforms vanilla: 9-class achieves DD OOD F1\,=\,0.818$\pm$0.096 (+53\,pp over vanilla 0.291$\pm$0.065), while MLM drops to vanilla level (0.289$\pm$0.101). On structurally complex ActorAttack, the advantage narrows (9-class 0.504$\pm$0.107 vs.\ vanilla 0.389$\pm$0.073, +11.5\,pp) with high seed variance, suggesting that limited per-source volume (250 per LLM) constrains generalization to complex attacks. DD and FITD thus primarily validate the baseline rather than the method; ActorAttack, where lexical methods collapse (TF-IDF F1\,=\,0.261) and vanilla encoders fail (F1\,$\leq$\,0.389 across conditions), provides the discriminative evaluation axis.
Mixed-LLM training confirms that classification supervision generalizes across LLM sources where unsupervised pretraining does not; full results in Appendix~\ref{app:mixed_llm}.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Human Data Validation}
\label{sec:human_data}

Since both training and OOD evaluation data are Qwen3-8B-generated, we validate on ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (204 human-written jailbreak attempts + 204 benign conversations from real LMSYS interactions).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Human data validation on ToxicChat~\citep{lin2023toxicchat} (macro F1, 3-seed mean$\pm$std). Bold indicates best. Single-turn data from real LMSYS user interactions, independent of Qwen3-8B.}
\label{tab:human_data}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & Macro F1 \\
\midrule
JB-MLM & \textbf{.837$\pm$.013} \\
Wiki-MLM & .791$\pm$.093 \\
Binary & .705$\pm$.072 \\
Scrambled & .616$\pm$.056 \\
9-class & .596$\pm$.087 \\
Topic & .496$\pm$.042 \\
\midrule
Vanilla & .413$\pm$.021 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All DAPT variants exceed vanilla by 18--42\,pp (Table~\ref{tab:human_data}), confirming that the adapted-vs.-vanilla gap is not a Qwen3-8B generation artifact: domain exposure on synthetic jailbreak text transfers to human-written attacks.

The ordering reverses: JB-MLM leads (0.837$\pm$0.013) while 9-class ranks lower (0.596$\pm$0.087; $p < 0.001$, non-overlapping CIs). ToxicChat is single-turn, so the classification head provides no advantage; validating the multi-turn hierarchy requires multi-turn human data.

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Perturbation Analysis}
\label{sec:perturbation}

Under adversarial paraphrasing (BERTScore 0.92), classification-supervised variants achieve zero degradation on IID and OOD DD (Table~\ref{tab:ood_perturbation}) while non-adapted models degrade by $\sim$12\,pp ($p < 0.001$); on ActorAttack, DAPT variants degrade ($\Delta$\,=\,$-$20.4\,pp) but maintain 52\,pp over vanilla (Appendix~\ref{sec:perturbation_full}).

%----------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Strategy Trajectory Analysis}
\label{sec:strategy}

The 9-class taxonomy provides interpretable characterization of known attacks ($\kappa$=0.78, $n$=50; Appendix~\ref{sec:strategy_full}) but degrades to near-random on OOD ($\kappa$=0.126; Appendix~\ref{app:strategy_pred}). Its value is as a training signal (scrambled labels produce equivalent detection) and IID characterization tool; detection operates through domain-adapted \texttt{[CLS]} embeddings, not strategy accuracy.

1	% introduction.tex — expanded for 8-page target
2	
3	\section{Introduction}
4	
5	Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns. Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} all rely on persuasion as their core mechanism: \citet{zeng2024pap} catalogue 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak families, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} identify strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. Because individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as benign text~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, no single-turn filter can distinguish them from legitimate conversation.
6	
7	Existing defenses leave a critical gap. Production classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and therefore miss manipulation that unfolds across exchanges. Multi-turn defenses have begun to model conversation-level structure: DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026} pairs fine-tuned BERT with a multi-layer GRU, BIID~\citep{tong2025biid} infers turn-level intentions, and G-Guard~\citep{gguard2025} applies graph neural networks. These systems achieve strong in-distribution performance, but each is evaluated on a single attack family. None answers the central question: \emph{what representation properties enable a detector to generalize across attack families it has never seen?}
8	
9	The simplest hypothesis is that pretrained language understanding already suffices. It does not, at least at base model scale. A vanilla DeBERTa-v3~\citep{he2021deberta} with temporal aggregation (cf.\ DeepContext) drops from F1\,=\,1.000 in-distribution to 0.312 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight. LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 reaches only 0.191--0.449 F1 with 30--47\% unparseable responses (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}). These failures share a root cause: neither model has been exposed to multi-turn adversarial text. The bottleneck is distributional, not architectural: cross-attack generalization requires domain adaptation, not a better classifier.
10	
11	We test this hypothesis through controlled ablation. Our pipeline, \textbf{DisPeD} (Disentangled Persuasion Detection), separates encoder adaptation (Stage~1) from temporal classification (Stage~2, a frozen BiGRU; Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}). Seven Stage~1 variants each test a single factor (e.g., domain exposure, label quality, temporal modeling) while holding all other components constant (Section~\ref{sec:method}). The contribution is the systematic decomposition of what enables cross-attack generalization, not the pipeline itself.

20	Controlled ablation across DeBERTa-v3 and RoBERTa~\citep{liu2019roberta} on four attack families and two training compositions shows that for base-size encoders (125--184M), classification-based adaptation is the most robust variant across synthetic multi-turn OOD attacks. Continued pretraining closes $\sim$60\,pp on single-source data but collapses on mixed-LLM training (DD OOD F1\,=\,0.818 vs.\ 0.291). This dependence diminishes with scale: RoBERTa-large (355M) handles even ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} without adaptation. A variance reduction of 4--20$\times$ is observed (3 seeds) for classification supervision on synthetic data but not on human-authored conversations (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}).
21	
22	Our contributions:
23	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
24	  \item \textbf{Systematic decomposition of cross-attack generalization.} Controlled ablation across thirteen encoder configurations, three OOD attack families, and two training compositions identifies classification-based domain adaptation as the most robust variant within synthetic multi-turn evaluation; unsupervised pretraining is effective on single-source data but collapses on mixed-LLM training. Three negative results are counter-intuitive: scrambled labels match correct labels, temporal order is irrelevant (mean pooling and turn-order shuffling confirm order-invariance across encoders), and label granularity does not affect detection.
25	
26	  \item \textbf{Capacity-dependent observation on domain adaptation.} Three encoder scales (125M, 184M, 355M) suggest that the set of attacks requiring adaptation shrinks with model size, though encoders differ in architecture and pretraining; RoBERTa-large handles structurally complex attacks without adaptation (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).
27	
28	  \item \textbf{Condition-dependent adaptation effects.} A variance reduction of 4--20$\times$ is observed (3 seeds) on synthetic data, but this benefit reverses on human-authored data. Mixed-LLM training validates that classification-based DAPT remains the strongest variant across training compositions, though the magnitude of advantage varies by attack complexity (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}). The 9-class taxonomy enables interpretable strategy characterization (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).
29	\end{itemize}
